doc.title: Sheryl Bailey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 24, 2023

title: Church-organist family, rock and heavy metal guitar, then harmony
summary: Bailey grew up in a family of church organists, fell for guitar, played Hendrix-style rock and metal, and was drawn to Berklee by wanting to understand harmony.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah, well yeah. When I was a teenager I — well I grew up in a family of professional — actually church organists really. And so we had to study piano and I’m telling you my — wherever she would be in the universe — if my piano teacher knew that I was a professional musician and educator she’d probably just, I don’t know, she’d be in shock. Because I was not a great piano student. But — maybe because everybody played at a really high level in my family and I don’t know, I was also a little younger, I was rebellious, and I saw the guitar and I just fell in love with the guitar so that was what I wanted to do. And of course guitar to a teenager is rock music. So I played what I guess is now called classic rock and blues originally, you know, I was into Hendrix and Robin Trower and all those kind of players out of that Hendrix school. And then I got into heavy metal, because I was a serious musician and at that time and mind of my teenage mind I was like well those folks are virtuosos so that’s the way to go. And then, and I still do, I call on that technique quite a bit in my project with Anat Cohen and the tentet project, you know there’s a sequence in there that’s all about just using that kind of technique and sound. So I mean I just kind of — I love guitar playing, virtuosic guitar playing in any genre. I’m not picky about that.

Did you have a period where you were playing some fairly technical music in that genre but you had yet to find out — I hesitate to say this because it sounds like an insult almost, but you didn’t know what you were doing from a musical standpoint from a chordal standpoint, music theory?

I think so. I mean I think that’s in everyone’s development for sure. Coming from a family of keyboard players, and I mean I mean harmony was so present in my imagination and musical world so I think that was the draw. I mean some of that actually, some of that neoclassical — they call it neoclassical shred is, they are Bach chord progressions and stuff. But did I know what it was? But that was what drew me to study at Berklee as a kid because I grew up with harmony and then you know that of course was an easy invitation into jazz and standards that I said I hear that but I don’t know what it’s called. And I still feel this way and I’m not rah-rah-rah Berklee, even though I’m associated there. But that’s what they do great is teach harmonic analysis, which — that was what I wanted to know. Because my ears — I never had perfect pitch, I have really good relative pitch but I said oh there are patterns there. What are those called? But I think that’s kind of everybody’s evolution in their musicianship at some point.
